subtopics.title: AI Concepts, Perspectives, History, Applications & Foundations
subtopics.subtitle: What AI is, the four perspectives, Turing test, milestones, applications and foundations

concepts.text: What Artificial Intelligence Is

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the branch of computer science concerned with building machines and programs that perform tasks which would require intelligence if done by humans: perceiving, reasoning, learning, planning, understanding language and acting in the world. The term was coined by John McCarthy in the 1955 proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project, held in 1956, which is regarded as the birth of AI as a field. Rich and Knight define AI as the study of how to make computers do things at which, at the moment, people are better. Modern textbooks such as Russell and Norvig define AI as the study and construction of rational agents.
The Four Perspectives on AI

Definitions of AI vary along two dimensions: whether they concern thought processes and reasoning or behaviour, and whether success is measured against human performance or against an ideal standard of rationality. Crossing the two dimensions gives four approaches. A system is rational if it does the right thing given what it knows.

rows: Thinking humanly: cognitive modelling; compare program traces with human thought (Newell and Simon's GPS, cognitive science)
Thinking rationally: laws of thought; Aristotle's syllogisms and formal logic used to derive correct conclusions
Acting humanly: the Turing test; behave so that an interrogator cannot tell the machine from a person
Acting rationally: the rational agent approach; act to achieve the best expected outcome (the focus of modern AI)

concepts.text: The Turing test (Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', 1950) and the capabilities it demands:
items: Setup (imitation game): a human interrogator exchanges typed questions with a hidden human and a hidden machine; the machine passes if the interrogator cannot reliably tell which is which.

Natural language processing to communicate, knowledge representation to store what it knows or hears, automated reasoning to answer questions and draw conclusions, and machine learning to adapt and detect patterns.
The total Turing test adds a video signal and the passing of physical objects, so it also requires computer vision (perception) and robotics (manipulation and movement).

Criticism: the test measures imitation of behaviour, not understanding; a program may pass by trickery (ELIZA-style pattern matching), and Searle's Chinese Room argues that symbol manipulation alone is not understanding.

concepts.plainText: Turing's prediction: an average interrogator has at most a 70% chance of correct identification after 5 minutes

concepts.text: Strong AI, Weak AI and Levels of Capability
Philosophical and practical classifications of AI:
items: Weak AI: machines can act as if they were intelligent; they simulate thinking and are useful tools, without any claim that they have minds.
Strong AI: an appropriately programmed machine would actually think and have a mind and consciousness, not merely simulate them (the position Searle's Chinese Room attacks).
Narrow AI (ANI): performs one specific task well, such as chess, face recognition or spam filtering; all deployed AI today is narrow.
General AI (AGI): human-level ability across any intellectual task; superintelligence (ASI) would exceed humans in all domains; both remain hypothetical.

concepts.text: History: Key Milestones

rows: McCulloch and Pitts model of the artificial neuron
First work now recognised as AI; threshold logic units
Proposes the Turing test, machine learning and genetic algorithms
Dartmouth conference (McCarthy, Minsky, Shannon, Rochester); Logic Theorist by Newell and Simon
Birth of AI; the name 'artificial intelligence' adopted
LISP (McCarthy), General Problem Solver, Rosenblatt's perceptron; Minsky and Papert's 'Perceptrons' (1969)
Early enthusiasm; limits of single-layer networks exposed
Lighthill report (1973), funding cuts; DENDRAL and MYCIN expert systems
First AI winter; shift to knowledge-based systems
XCON (R1) at DEC, Japan's Fifth Generation project; backpropagation popularised (1986); collapse of the expert-system market late in the decade
Expert-system boom, neural-network revival, second AI winter
Deep Blue beats Kasparov (1997), IBM Watson wins Jeopardy! (2011), AlexNet (2012), AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol (2016)
Probabilistic methods, big data and deep learning

concepts.text: Applications of AI
Representative application areas:
items: Game playing (chess, Go, poker), robotics and autonomous vehicles, planning and scheduling (NASA's Remote Agent, logistics planning).
Expert systems for diagnosis and configuration (MYCIN, DENDRAL, XCON); medical image analysis; fraud detection and credit scoring.
Natural language processing: machine translation, speech recognition, chatbots and question answering; computer vision: face recognition, OCR, surveillance.
Spam filtering, recommendation systems, search engines, smart assistants and industrial process control.

concepts.text: Foundations of AI

rows: Can formal rules draw valid conclusions? How does the mind arise from the brain?
Logic, methods of reasoning, rationalism, mind as a physical system, foundations of learning
What can be computed? How do we reason with uncertain information?
Formal logic, algorithms, computability and incompleteness, tractability and NP-completeness, probability
How should we decide to maximise payoff?
Utility, decision theory, game theory, operations research
Study of neurons and the nervous system; inspiration for neural networks
How do humans and animals think and act?
Behaviourism, cognitive psychology, the brain as an information-processing device
How can we build an efficient computer?
The hardware (and software tools) on which AI programs run
How can artifacts operate under their own control? How does language relate to thought?
Feedback, objective functions, cybernetics (Wiener); grammars and knowledge representation (Chomsky)

concepts.plainText: Rational action a* = the action that maximises expected performance given the percept sequence and built-in knowledge

formulas.plainText: a* = argmax over actions of expected performance given percepts and knowledge
Turing's 1950 prediction: interrogator correct at most 70% of the time after 5 minutes

notes.text: Match each perspective to its keyword: thinking humanly = cognitive modelling, acting humanly = Turing test, thinking rationally = laws of thought (logic, syllogisms), acting rationally = rational agent. The rational agent approach is the one modern AI adopts.

The standard Turing test needs no vision or robotics because the interaction is by text only; those two capabilities belong to the total Turing test. Also, 1950 is Turing's paper, 1956 is the Dartmouth conference; do not swap them.

Astrology, alchemy and similar fields are never listed among the foundations; the accepted list is philosophy, mathematics, economics, neuroscience, psychology, computer engineering, control theory and cybernetics, and linguistics.

formulas.title: Rational action
formulas.plainText: a* = argmax_a E[performance | percept sequence, knowledge]
formulas.description: Acting rationally means choosing the action with the highest expected performance given what the agent has perceived and knows.

formulas.title: Turing's prediction
formulas.description: Turing predicted that by about 2000 an average interrogator would have no more than a 70% chance of identifying the machine after five minutes of questioning.

questions.questionText: Compared with the standard Turing test, the total Turing test additionally requires the machine to have:
options: Natural language processing and automated reasoning
questions.explanation: The total Turing test adds a video signal and physical object passing, so the machine needs computer vision to perceive and robotics to manipulate; NLP, knowledge representation, reasoning and learning are already needed for the text-only test.

questions.questionText: The claim that an appropriately programmed computer does not merely simulate a mind but actually has a mind and understands is known as:
options: The physical symbol system hypothesis being false
questions.explanation: Strong AI holds that the right program genuinely thinks; weak AI only claims machines can act as if intelligent. Searle's Chinese Room argument is directed against strong AI.

questions.questionText: Which sequence lists these AI events in correct chronological order?
options: Dartmouth conference, Turing's 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence', Deep Blue beats Kasparov, Lighthill report
Lighthill report, Dartmouth conference, Turing's paper, Deep Blue beats Kasparov
Turing's paper, Lighthill report, Dartmouth conference, Deep Blue beats Kasparov
Turing's paper, Dartmouth conference, Lighthill report, Deep Blue beats Kasparov

subtopics.title: Intelligent Agents: Structure, Properties & PEAS
subtopics.subtitle: Agents, percepts, agent function vs program, rationality, autonomy and PEAS tables

concepts.text: Agents and Environments

An agent is anything that perceives its environment through sensors and acts upon that environment through actuators. A human agent has eyes and ears as sensors and hands, legs and voice as actuators; a robot has cameras and range finders as sensors and motors as actuators; a software agent (softbot) receives keystrokes, files and network packets and acts by displaying output, writing files or sending packets. The agent repeatedly runs the cycle sensors → percepts → agent function → actions → actuators.
Key terms:
items: Percept: the agent's perceptual input at a given instant.
Percept sequence: the complete history of everything the agent has ever perceived; an agent's choice of action can depend on the whole percept sequence but not on anything it has not perceived.
Agent function: an abstract mathematical mapping from every possible percept sequence to an action; it describes the agent's behaviour externally.
Agent program: the concrete implementation of the agent function that runs on a physical system; it takes the current percept as input.
Architecture: the computing device with physical sensors and actuators on which the program runs (a PC, a robotic car, a phone).

concepts.plainText: Agent function f maps percept sequences P* to actions A

concepts.text: A table-driven agent implements the agent function literally by storing the action for every possible percept sequence in a lookup table. With |P| possible percepts and a lifetime of T percepts the table needs the sum of |P|^t for t = 1 to T entries, which becomes astronomically large (a chess table would need more entries than atoms in the universe). The design problem of AI is therefore to write small programs that produce rational behaviour without such a table.

function TABLE-DRIVEN-AGENT(percept) returns an action
  persistent: percepts, a sequence, initially empty
              table, indexed by percept sequences, fully specified
  append percept to the end of percepts
  action <- LOOKUP(percepts, table)
  return action
Rationality and Autonomy

A rational agent is one that does the right thing. For each possible percept sequence, a rational agent selects an action that is expected to maximise its performance measure, given the evidence provided by the percept sequence and whatever built-in knowledge it has. What is rational at any time depends on four things: the performance measure defining success, the agent's prior knowledge of the environment, the actions it can perform, and its percept sequence to date.
Rationality is not perfection:
items: Rationality is not omniscience: an omniscient agent knows the actual outcome of its actions; a rational agent maximises expected performance and can still suffer bad luck.
Information gathering (looking before crossing a road) and exploration are part of rational behaviour when the environment is not fully known.
Learning: a rational agent should learn as much as possible from what it perceives and modify its behaviour accordingly.
Autonomy: an agent is autonomous to the extent that its behaviour is determined by its own experience rather than only by the designer's built-in knowledge.

concepts.text: Properties commonly required of intelligent agents:
items: Autonomy: operates without direct human intervention and controls its own actions and internal state.
Reactivity: perceives the environment and responds in a timely way to changes in it.
Pro-activeness: exhibits goal-directed behaviour by taking the initiative rather than only reacting.
Social ability: interacts with other agents and humans through some agent-communication language; further properties often listed are learning (adaptivity), mobility and rationality.

concepts.text: PEAS Description of the Task Environment

Before designing an agent, its task environment is specified with PEAS: Performance measure (the criterion of success, defined on environment states, not on how the agent feels), Environment (what the agent operates in), Actuators (how it acts) and Sensors (how it perceives). A good performance measure rewards what one actually wants in the environment rather than how one thinks the agent should behave.

rows: Safe, fast, legal, comfortable trip; maximise profits
Percentage of parts placed in correct bins
Roads, other traffic, pedestrians, customers, weather
Steering, accelerator, brake, signal, horn, display
Display of questions, tests, diagnoses, treatments, referrals
Cameras, sonar, speedometer, GPS, odometer, accelerometer, engine sensors
Keyboard entry of symptoms, findings, patient's answers
Dirt sensor, bump sensor, location sensor

formulas.plainText: Table entries = sum over t = 1..T of |P|^t

notes.text: In PEAS items, classify each phrase by role: what is measured is P, where the agent lives is E, what it outputs or moves is A, and what it reads or senses is S. 'Keyboard entry of symptoms' is a sensor for a diagnosis system; 'display of diagnoses' is an actuator.

Do not confuse the agent function (an abstract mapping over entire percept sequences) with the agent program (code that receives only the current percept and must remember history itself if it needs it).

Rational does not mean omniscient or successful: an agent that looked both ways and was then hit by a falling object still acted rationally, because it maximised expected performance on the information available.

formulas.title: Agent composition
formulas.description: An agent is the agent program running on an architecture that supplies the physical sensors and actuators.

formulas.title: Agent function
formulas.description: The agent function maps every possible percept sequence to the action the agent takes.

formulas.title: Table-driven agent size
formulas.description: A lookup-table agent with |P| possible percepts over a lifetime of T steps needs one entry for every percept sequence of length 1 to T.

flashcards.back: Performance measure, Environment, Actuators and Sensors; it specifies an agent's task environment.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between the agent function and the agent program?
flashcards.back: The agent function is an abstract mapping from percept sequences to actions; the agent program is the concrete code that implements it on an architecture, taking the current percept as input.

flashcards.front: On what four things does rationality depend?
flashcards.back: The performance measure, the agent's prior knowledge of the environment, the actions available to it, and its percept sequence to date.

flashcards.front: When is an agent called autonomous?
flashcards.back: When its behaviour is determined by its own experience and learning rather than relying only on the designer's built-in knowledge.

questions.questionText: A table-driven agent can receive 4 distinct percepts and will run for a lifetime of 3 percepts. How many entries must its lookup table hold to cover every possible percept sequence?
questions.explanation: The table needs an entry for every percept sequence of length 1, 2 and 3: 4 + 4^2 + 4^3 = 4 + 16 + 64 = 84.

questions.questionText: In the PEAS description of a medical diagnosis system, which item is an actuator?
options: Keyboard entry of symptoms and patient's answers
Display of questions, tests, diagnoses, treatments and referrals
questions.explanation: The system acts on its environment by displaying questions, tests, diagnoses and referrals; keyboard entry is its sensor, a healthy patient is the performance measure and the hospital setting is the environment.

questions.questionText: A delivery robot checks for traffic, sees the road is clear and starts crossing, but is struck by debris falling from an aircraft. According to the definition of rationality, the robot:
options: Acted rationally, because rationality maximises expected performance given the percepts, not actual outcomes
Acted irrationally, because a rational agent always achieves the best actual outcome
Acted irrationally, because it was not omniscient
Cannot be judged, because rationality applies only to software agents
questions.explanation: Rationality is judged on expected performance given the percept sequence and prior knowledge; it is not omniscience, so an unforeseeable event does not make the choice irrational.

subtopics.title: Types of Agents: Simple Reflex, Model-Based, Goal-Based & Utility-Based
subtopics.subtitle: Four agent programs from reflex rules to utility maximisation, plus learning agents

concepts.text: Agent Programs from Simple to Complex

Russell and Norvig describe four basic kinds of agent program, in order of increasing generality: simple reflex agents, model-based reflex agents, goal-based agents and utility-based agents. Any of these can be turned into a learning agent that improves its performance over time. Each type keeps the agent cycle of perceiving and acting but differs in what it stores internally and how it chooses an action.
Simple Reflex Agent

A simple reflex agent selects actions on the basis of the current percept only, ignoring the rest of the percept history. It uses condition-action rules (if-then rules), for example 'if car-in-front-is-braking then initiate-braking'. It is simple and fast but works correctly only if the right decision can be made from the current percept, that is, only if the environment is fully observable. In partially observable environments it can fall into infinite loops, which randomising its actions can sometimes escape.

function SIMPLE-REFLEX-AGENT(percept) returns an action
  persistent: rules, a set of condition-action rules
  state  <- INTERPRET-INPUT(percept)
  rule   <- RULE-MATCH(state, rules)
  action <- rule.ACTION
  return action
Model-Based Reflex Agent

A model-based reflex agent handles partial observability by keeping an internal state that depends on the percept history and reflects unobserved aspects of the world. Updating this state needs a model of the world: knowledge of how the world evolves independently of the agent and of how the agent's own actions affect the world. It still chooses actions with condition-action rules, but matches them against its internal state rather than the raw percept.

function MODEL-BASED-REFLEX-AGENT(percept) returns an action
  persistent: state, model, rules, action (most recent, initially none)
  state  <- UPDATE-STATE(state, action, percept, model)
  rule   <- RULE-MATCH(state, rules)
  action <- rule.ACTION
  return action
Goal-Based and Utility-Based Agents

A goal-based agent has, in addition to a model, explicit goal information describing desirable situations. It considers the future, asking 'what will happen if I do action A?', and uses search and planning to find action sequences that achieve the goal. It is more flexible than a reflex agent because its knowledge is explicit and can be changed simply by changing the goal, but goals give only a binary distinction between happy and unhappy states.

A utility-based agent uses a utility function that maps a state (or sequence of states) to a real number describing the degree of happiness. It chooses the action that maximises expected utility, averaging over the possible outcomes weighted by their probabilities. Utility lets the agent trade off conflicting goals (speed against safety) and weigh the likelihood of success against the importance of goals when none can be achieved with certainty.

concepts.latex: EU(a) = \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, a)\, U(s'), \quad a^{*} = \arg\max_{a} EU(a)
concepts.plainText: EU(a) = sum over s' of P(s'|s,a) U(s'); choose a* = argmax EU(a)

rows: Search or planning towards an explicit goal
Tasks with clear goal states (route finding)

concepts.text: Learning Agents
A learning agent has four conceptual components:
items: Performance element: selects external actions; it is what the other four agent types consist of entirely.
Critic: observes the world and tells the learning element how well the agent is doing with respect to a fixed performance standard.
Learning element: responsible for making improvements, using feedback from the critic to modify the performance element.
Problem generator: suggests exploratory actions that lead to new and informative experiences, even if they are suboptimal in the short run.

concepts.text: Learning lets an agent start in an initially unknown environment and become more competent than its initial knowledge alone would allow. For a taxi, the performance element drives, the critic notices that other drivers honk after a sudden lane change, the learning element adds a rule against such changes, and the problem generator might propose testing the brakes on different road surfaces.

formulas.plainText: EU(a) = sum over s' of P(s'|s,a) U(s')

notes.text: Keyword map for agent-type MCQs: 'current percept only / condition-action rules' = simple reflex; 'internal state / partially observable' = model-based; 'what will happen if / goal / planning' = goal-based; 'how happy / degree of desirability / trade-off' = utility-based; 'critic / problem generator' = learning agent.

A model-based reflex agent still decides by condition-action rules; having a model does not make it goal-based. Goal-based agents look ahead at the consequences of actions, which reflex agents never do.
The critic is needed because percepts alone give no indication of success; the performance standard is fixed outside the agent so that the agent cannot adjust the standard to suit its own behaviour.

formulas.title: Expected utility
formulas.description: A utility-based agent scores each action by averaging the utility of its possible outcome states weighted by their probabilities.

formulas.title: Maximum expected utility choice
formulas.description: The rational utility-based agent selects the action with the highest expected utility.

formulas.title: Model-based state update
formulas.description: A model-based agent combines its previous internal state, last action, new percept and world model to estimate the current state.

flashcards.front: Why does a simple reflex agent need a fully observable environment?
flashcards.back: It decides only from the current percept with condition-action rules and keeps no memory, so it acts correctly only if the current percept reveals everything relevant.

flashcards.front: What two kinds of knowledge make up the world model of a model-based agent?
flashcards.back: How the world evolves independently of the agent, and how the agent's own actions change the world.

flashcards.front: What advantage does a utility-based agent have over a goal-based agent?
flashcards.back: Its utility function gives degrees of desirability, so it can trade off conflicting goals and weigh probability of success rather than only distinguishing goal from non-goal states.

flashcards.front: Name the four components of a learning agent.
flashcards.back: Performance element, critic, learning element and problem generator.

questions.questionText: In a learning agent, which component compares the agent's behaviour against a fixed performance standard and provides feedback to the learning element?
questions.explanation: The critic judges how well the agent is doing relative to a fixed performance standard and feeds this back to the learning element; the performance element selects actions and the problem generator proposes exploratory actions.

questions.questionText: A utility-based taxi agent can take Route A or Route B. Route A arrives on time with probability 0.9 (utility 80) and late with probability 0.1 (utility 20). Route B arrives on time with probability 0.6 (utility 100) and late with probability 0.4 (utility 40). Which route does the agent choose, and with what expected utility?
questions.explanation: EU(A) = 0.9 × 80 + 0.1 × 20 = 72 + 2 = 74 and EU(B) = 0.6 × 100 + 0.4 × 40 = 60 + 16 = 76, so the agent picks Route B with expected utility 76.

subtopics.title: Environment Types & Properties
subtopics.subtitle: Observable, deterministic, episodic, static, discrete, agents and known, with examples

concepts.text: Why Environment Properties Matter

The range of task environments is vast, but they can be categorised along a small number of dimensions. These properties largely determine the appropriate agent design: a fully observable, deterministic, static, discrete, single-agent environment is the easiest, while a partially observable, stochastic, sequential, dynamic, continuous, multi-agent environment such as taxi driving is the hardest case.
Observability and number of agents:
items: Fully observable: the sensors give access to the complete relevant state of the environment at each point in time, so the agent need not keep internal state (crossword, chess).

Partially observable (semi-observable): noisy or inaccurate sensors, or parts of the state are missing from the data (a vacuum agent with only a local dirt sensor, poker, taxi); unobservable if the agent has no sensors at all.
Single agent: only one agent acts (solving a crossword alone).

Multi-agent: other agents whose behaviour affects this agent's performance; competitive (chess, where one maximises while the other minimises) or cooperative (taxis avoiding collisions); communication and randomised behaviour can become rational.

concepts.text: Determinism, episodes and time:
items: Deterministic: the next state is completely determined by the current state and the agent's action; otherwise stochastic (outcomes quantified by probabilities) or nondeterministic (possible outcomes listed without probabilities).
Strategic: deterministic except for the actions of other agents (chess is often classed this way).

Episodic: experience is divided into atomic episodes; in each the agent perceives and performs one action, and the choice in one episode does not affect the next (defect detection on an assembly line, image classification).
Sequential: the current decision can affect all future decisions (chess, taxi driving), so the agent must think ahead.

concepts.text: Change, representation and knowledge:
items: Static: the environment does not change while the agent is deliberating (crossword).
Dynamic: the environment keeps changing while the agent deliberates; not deciding counts as deciding to do nothing (taxi driving).
Semi-dynamic: the environment itself does not change with time but the agent's performance score does (chess played with a clock).
Discrete vs continuous: applies to states, time, percepts and actions; chess has a finite number of distinct states and moves, whereas taxi speed, position and steering angle vary continuously.

Known vs unknown: refers to the agent's (or designer's) knowledge of the rules of the environment; in an unknown environment the agent must learn how it works. A known environment can be partially observable (solitaire) and an unknown one can be fully observable (a new video game).

concepts.plainText: Deterministic: s' = RESULT(s, a); Stochastic: probability P(s'|s, a) over next states

concepts.text: Classification of Example Environments

The classifications in these tables follow Russell and Norvig and depend on how the task is defined. Medical diagnosis is single-agent because the patient is modelled as part of the environment, not as an agent maximising its own performance; image analysis is semi-dynamic because the image does not change but slow analysis may be penalised; poker is stochastic because the deal of cards is random.
The Vacuum-Cleaner World

The two-square vacuum world is the standard small example. The agent can be in square A or B, and each square can be clean or dirty, so there are 2 × 2^2 = 8 world states. If the agent senses both its location and the dirt status of every square, the world is fully observable; with only a local dirt sensor it becomes partially observable. If sucking always cleans, it is deterministic; if dirt can reappear or suction sometimes fails, it becomes stochastic.

concepts.plainText: Number of states of an n-square vacuum world = n x 2^n (n = 2 gives 8)

formulas.plainText: Deterministic: s' = RESULT(s, a); Stochastic: P(s'|s, a)
Sum over s' of P(s'|s, a) = 1

notes.text: Memorise the hardest case, taxi driving: partially observable, multi-agent, stochastic, sequential, dynamic, continuous. The easiest case is a crossword puzzle: fully observable, single agent, deterministic, sequential, static, discrete.

Semi-dynamic is not the same as dynamic: in chess with a clock the board does not change while a player thinks, only the score (time remaining) does. Also 'semi-observable' in the syllabus means partially observable.

Known versus unknown describes knowledge of the environment's rules (the transition model), while fully versus partially observable describes what the sensors reveal about the current state; the two dimensions are independent.

formulas.title: Deterministic vs stochastic transition
formulas.plainText: Deterministic: s' = RESULT(s, a); Stochastic: P(s'|s, a)
formulas.description: In a deterministic environment an action has exactly one outcome; in a stochastic one it leads to a probability distribution over next states.

formulas.title: Normalisation of outcomes
formulas.description: In a stochastic environment the probabilities of all possible next states after an action must add up to one.

formulas.title: Vacuum world state count
formulas.description: With n squares, the agent has n possible locations and each square is clean or dirty, giving 8 states for the two-square world.

flashcards.front: What is a semi-dynamic environment? Give an example.
flashcards.back: One in which the environment does not change with time but the agent's performance score does; chess played with a clock.

flashcards.front: How is taxi driving classified on all six main environment dimensions?
flashcards.back: Partially observable, multi-agent, stochastic, sequential, dynamic and continuous.
In an episodic environment each episode's action does not affect later episodes; in a sequential environment the current decision can affect all future decisions.

flashcards.front: How many states does the two-square vacuum world have?
flashcards.back: 8: two agent locations times four clean/dirty combinations of the squares (2 × 2^2).

questions.questionText: Which of the following task environments is episodic rather than sequential?
questions.explanation: In image analysis each classification is an independent episode that does not affect the next; chess, taxi driving and poker are sequential because current decisions affect future ones.

questions.questionText: In chess played with a clock, the board does not change while a player is thinking, but the time remaining does affect the player's performance. This environment is best described as:
questions.explanation: An environment is semi-dynamic when the environment itself does not change with the passage of time but the agent's performance score does, which is exactly the case for chess with a clock.
